I remember uttering a very interesting, and I think important, phrase to a friend when four of us were hanging out one day.

We were all gathered and fiddling with musical instruments and exchanging good conversation.

One my friends started to get rather anxious and started asking some rather strange questions, things that wouldn't be easily answered or that were so theoretical you might as well just wait till the moment to see what happens.

Now I may have done a poor job explaining how he was acting but I remember this phrase passing my lips without thinking.

"Stop living in other moments."

Now I'm not saying you don't think about the future or contemplate and learn from the past. But remember that even when you are doing so you should stay grounded in the current moment.

I ask for your help in dissecting this as I don't feel as solid in my explanation. Please dig in and let me know what you think.

I think it really depends on the person. For instance, some people view and approach the world from a more concrete perspective of reality, while others view the world and approach it from a much more abstract and theoretical standpoint. In a similar vein, a person's reality might be shaped mainly by externally motivated perceptions, while another's sense of reality might be shaped predominately by internally motivated perceptions, or by the interface between the two.

What you refer to as 'living in other moments' is different from person to person, and although it could be detrimental for some people, I think for others it's natural. When you consider visionaries and inventors and innovators, they forged new paths by living in other moments, by looking at our present reality and thinking of ways to improve it in unforeseen ways. That type of mindset isn't for everyone, but I think it's necessary for progress, and I think it comes naturally to some people, so it shouldn't be discouraged.

I'm the person in friend groups who's more interested in talking about deeper, cerebral subjects on huge time scales (because that's how I naturally think – I can't help but think of possible futures because that's the scale of context my mind naturally gravitates towards, and I don't mind it), but I've accepted that most people I come across are not necessarily into that type of conversation. Having said that, I don't think there's anything wrong with wanting to talk about abstractions, I think it's just a matter of knowing the right time and place to do it, and the right people to do it with. It sounds like your friend is either not used to thinking this way, or might have just chosen the wrong time to bring it up?

Ahhh. Fresh perspective. It may have simply been a timing thing. That group of friends does tend to go pretty deep into a conversation though.

I like your perspectives on grand time scales and what changes now could mean for the future.

I'd have to say that while some new paths can be forged through other moments, you must also realize your own perspective is unique and if you follow it wholeheartedly you are most likely forging a new path naturally. That may sounds strange but the idea that each person's perspective has a uniqueness to it means that by simply living in your moment you'll most likely forge something completely novel. Again that doesn't remove contemplating the earth, the human race and what things may come to be...

I feel I'm having a hard time because I'd say I live in the moment but yet that includes thinking about all these things as well.

Now when you speak of externally motivated perceptions for some reason I tend to think of it as an unnatural state. As in you haven't quite been grounded yet but you'll eventually get there. One perspective seems too limited for this but I enjoy the philosophical nature of it all.

Heh it doesn't sound strange that you think that way, it just means that you and I come at our perceptions of reality from different places. I look at the fascinating qualities of sameness we all share and find it easy to think on the scale of humanity as a whole, whereas you look at the beautiful differences between us as individuals and find it easy to think on a more personal scale. They're both valid ways of experiencing the word.

As for internally versus externally motivated perception, I probably could have used a better way of phrasing those. As an example, if you take a concept like 'justice' and ask a few people what it means to them, one person's response might entail justice on the scale of humanity, whereas someone else's answer might focus on justice within the context of societies and cultures relative to each other, and yet others might focus their interpretation of justice as a purely internal construct that varies from person to person. A person who thinks that justice can't be truly pinned down beyond the individual level would be someone I consider to have more of internally motivated perception. Someone who thinks of it on the scale of humanity would be someone who I think has a more externally motivated perception.
